    A gun battle between Mexican soldiers and alleged gang members in the city of Guasave, in the state of Sinaloa, ended with special forces detaining senior members of the Beltran Leyva drug trafficking network, Mexican officials said on Saturday.

    The gang is aligned with one of the factions of the powerful Sinaloa cartel.

    Authorities stated the overnight raid resulted in capture of the suspected drug kingpin Fausto Isidro Meza F., better known as "Chapo Isidro," who is believed to be the leader of Beltran Leyva.

    The 44-year-old Mexican national is one of the FBI's ten most wanted fugitives. The US law enforcement agency claims his group is responsible for smuggling "large quantities of heroin, methamphetamine, cocaine, fentanyl, and marijuana into the United States," and has offered a $5 million (€4.56 million) reward for information leading to his arrest.

    He is also wanted in Mexico on charges including organized crime.

    On Saturday, Mexican authorities said the raid was conducted due to "intelligence coordination" between Mexico's military and US agencies.

    The three detainees were transported to Mexico City "to be placed at the disposal of the competent prosecutorial authorities," the military said.

    It was not immediately clear if "Chapo Isidro" will be extradited to the US.

    The troops used "stealth and surprise" to reach the area, establishing a perimeter around the drug dealer's location and then moving in from multiple directions, according Mexico's US embassy.

    Unverified videos from Guasave, however, highlighted military helicopters firing at ground targets and sports fans scrambling for safety during a baseball game. Some of the violence in the western Mexican city seems to have taken place after Chapo Isidro was arrested, with drug cartels attempting to retaliate against the authorities and civilians for the move.

    Mexico's defense ministry confirmed cartel members set up roadblocks in the area, but added that security forces were assisting local authorities in restoring order.

    The Guasave raid is only the latest in a string of high-profile moves against senior leaders of Mexico's illegal drug trade. Less than two weeks ago, Mexican navy announced the arrest of Rafael A., suspected of leading a cartel cell active in the states of Jalisco and Michoacan.

    President ​Claudia Sheinbaum is facing pressure from Donald Trump, who has threatened to take military action against cartels on Mexican territory.

    Breaking: Fight over fossil fuels leaves COP31 climate talks in deadlock

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (917 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Co

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Panama's Environment Minister is pushing for language on fossil fuels to be in the final agreement.
    • Negotiations at the COP31 UN climate summit in Turkey are in deadlock and have been suspended for the night, after running more than a day over time, as countries have been unable to agree on a upcoming global climate deal.
    • The EU and Pacific island nations are amongst a group pushing back against the latest draft agreement which included no reference to reducing the world's demand for fossil fuels.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Panama's Environment Minister is pushing for language on fossil fuels to be in the final agreement.

    Negotiations at the COP31 UN climate summit in Turkey are in deadlock and have been suspended for the night, after running more than a day over time, as countries have been unable to agree on a upcoming global climate deal.

    The EU and Pacific island nations are amongst a group pushing back against the latest draft agreement which included no reference to reducing the world's demand for fossil fuels.

    A second sticking point involves a push from the Africa Group to get commitments on more money for adaptation - but the EU has previously said it would not support this.

    Negotiating teams due to fly out on Sunday morning are now moving their flights to Monday in a sign that a deal is not yet in sight.

    If countries cannot reach consensus - which is required by the UN's climate talks process - the negotiations could be suspended.

    Sources indicate that in that case the summit would end with no deal and be reconvened next year. This has only happened once before since countries started holding COP climate meetings in 1995.

    Recent findings suggest that on Saturday, EU Commissioner for Climate Wopke Hoekstra said if the bloc could not get "what is needed in terms of climate action... then there's no deal.".

    The UK's chief negotiator, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, remained more hopeful and said her team was still working to get an agreement.

    "These are difficult negotiations, but discussions remain productive and there is a deal to be done. The UK is pushing hard for an outcome and we will keep working in the coming hours to bring countries together.".

    Another risk is that negotiating teams have to start journeys home, and the meeting could lose the critical number of nations needed to pass any global agreement.

    Sources indicate that more climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged.

    Ministers from Panama, Solomon Islands, Cote d'Ivoire and the EU are fighting to get a commitment to move away from oil, gas and coal back into the final agreement after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi Arabia pushed for its removal.

    "It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.

    His words were echoed by France's Minister of Ecological Transition, Monique Barbut.

    She took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture, use and storage - the technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground - as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.

    "We cannot be announcing to the world that we are now getting to 1.5 increase in the temperature and do business like nothing was happening," Barbut noted.

    For the first time at a COP the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - could acknowledge that the goal of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed.

    The world is entering a period called "overshoot".

    Beyond this point scientists warn, external that millions more people will be exposed to sea level rise and extreme heat.

    But Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister who is leading negotiations, pushed back on the need to include language on fossil fuels.

    He argued that this summit was about implementation, and should focus on the move towards clean energy sources.

    According to recent reports, away from COP, renewable energy is growing at unprecedented rates. For the first time this year a modern renewable source - solar panels - was the biggest contributor to meeting upcoming global energy demand, outstripping oil and gas, external.

    The International Energy Agency also warned this week that the longer disruption to fuel supplies through the Strait of Hormuz due to the Iran War continues, the stronger the incentive to switch to electricity powered by renewables.

    Although, this week US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin agreed at a meeting in Shenzhen to increase oil production in the face of fuel supply disruption.

    It is understood that one proposal is to keep fossil fuels off the table in exchange for Saudi Arabia and other petro-states signing up to a pledge for 35% of their energy consumption to come from electricity by 2035.

    This does not solve one of the other key problems raised by developing nations - the lack of money.

    Earlier versions of the text included an agreement to ramp up money for adaptation to $120bn (Â£91bn) by 2035 - that figure has now been removed.

    "We did not come here to beg, we came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries," said Zanetor Agyeman Rawlings, Ghana's Environment Minister and chair of the African Group of negotiators.

    Climate activists and environmental groups, who are observers to these talks, have slammed negotiations.

    "I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever," said Mohamed Adow of Powershift Africa.

    According to recent reports, these groups are normally highly critical of the process for not moving fast enough. But it seems that Turkey have been particularly unpopular as co-hosts after their lead negotiator walked out of some crucial negotiations leaving many countries feeling "disrespected", remarked one observer.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (716 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theguardian ↗ Open Full Page

    Race to replant five South African baobabs after export blocked

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (716 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits.
    • Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.
    • It has been revealed that the baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The trees, intended for an unnamed buyer in Georgia, were reportedly dug up without the necessary permits.

    Environmentalists in South Africa are racing to replant five centuries-old baobabs after the 20-tonne trees were dug up by an exporter, who tried to ship them thousands of miles to Georgia.

    It has been revealed that the baobabs arrived at a reserve in Timbavati, in north-eastern South Africa, on Wednesday, where they will be replanted and supported by cables to help them recover. The trees had been stranded at a warehouse in Durban since July, when they were intercepted by authorities who mentioned they had been moved without the necessary permissions.

    The department of forestry, fisheries and the environment confirmed the trees had been destined for Georgia but did not name the buyer.

    It has been revealed that the case echoes an episode in Kenya four years ago, when eight baobabs were uprooted to be exported to Shekvetili Dendrological Park, owned by Bidzina Ivanishvili, an influential Georgian billionaire and the country’s former prime minister. Ivanishvili has filled the park with ancient, giant trees from Georgia, transporting them by boat along the Black Sea.

    The export of the Kenyan baobabs was initially blocked after an outcry by environmentalists, who condemned their export as biopiracy, but later allowed to go ahead.

    Recent findings suggest that otherwise, such exports are very rare, say experts. David Newton, programme office director for east and southern Africa for Traffic, an NGO that monitors the trade in wild animals and plants, said: “It is very unusual to see baobabs being used as ornamental plants … mainly because they are exceptionally difficult to dig out of the ground and transport, and then to successfully re-establish.”.

    Industry observers note that sarah Venter, founder of the Baobab Foundation, who has led efforts to replant the South African trees, noted she believes they have a good chance of surviving if they are replanted rapidly. The winter months of May to October, when the trees lose their leaves and are dormant, is a good time to move them.

    “As soon as spring starts [in November], the trees use their water to flush their new leaves, and that’s when we need to get them into the ground as soon as possible,” she said.

    The rescue mission has faced delays because of the challenges associated with moving such large trees, which are transported on special trucks capable of carrying abnormal loads. The five baobabs weigh between 19 and 29 tonnes, have a diameter of up to 4.5 metres (15ft) and a height of up to 12.5 metres.

    Baobabs, known as the tree of life, are protected under South African law, which means a permit is required to cut or disturb them.

    It has been revealed that “A baobab isn’t just part of an ecosystem, it is an ecosystem in itself,” said Wambui Ippolito, a landscape designer, lecturer and horticulturist from Kenya. “These trees are biodiversity anchors.”.

    Animals ranging from bats and bush babies, to grey-headed parrots and the southern ground hornbill shelter in its cavities, while elephants, monkeys and warthogs feast on its fruit.

    It has been revealed that the trees have huge cultural importance, added Ippolito. “It has always been a sacred tree in Africa. It doesn’t matter where you go: Senegal, Mali, Ghana – wherever you go, if there is a community around a baobab tree, that tree is sacred,” she said. “Somebody’s great-great-great-great-great-grandparents sat under that tree, and it is part of human history in that area.”.

    According to recent reports, baobabs have shallow roots, which means they do not need to be planted very deeply, and these regrow fairly quickly, said Venter. Once replanted, the trees will be stabilised with cables and protected by electric fences to prevent damage from elephants.

    The trees are thought to be between 200 and 300 years old. “Baobabs easily reach 1,000 years old, so they’ve got a few hundred years ahead of them if they survive,” noted Venter.

    A criminal case has been opened against the owner of a landscaping company allegedly responsible for the illegal harvesting and transportation of the trees.

    Find more age of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reporters Rebecca Ratcliffe, Phoebe Weston and Patrick Greenfield in the Guardian app for more nature coverage.

    #81895. Industry News: Getting rid of antibiotic resistance: Challenges and possible solutions

    📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (875 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Getting rid of antibiotic resistance: Challenges and possible solutions

    📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (875 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that "The threat is immense," said Jean Pierre Nyemazi, acting director of the World Health Organization's department of antimicrobial resistance, during a virtual press conference  recently.
    • It has been revealed that it was, however, the stated goal of World Health Organization, or WHO, member statesto reduce the mortality rate caused by AMR by 10% until 2030, Nyemazi added.
    • A world without effective antibiotics would be like traveling back to the days in which even the smallest infection was life-threatening, mentioned Can Imirzalioglu, director of the Institute of Medical Microbiology at Justus Liebig University Giessen.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that "The threat is immense," said Jean Pierre Nyemazi, acting director of the World Health Organization's department of antimicrobial resistance, during a virtual press conference  recently. "An estimated cumulative number of 39 million deaths directly attributable to AMR [antimicrobial resistance] would occur in the next 25 years.".

    It has been revealed that it was, however, the stated goal of World Health Organization, or WHO, member statesto reduce the mortality rate caused by AMR by 10% until 2030, Nyemazi added. "When we see the trend, the investments, the action, we don't think we are on the right track.".

    A world without effective antibiotics would be like traveling back to the days in which even the smallest infection was life-threatening, mentioned Can Imirzalioglu, director of the Institute of Medical Microbiology at Justus Liebig University Giessen. "If antibiotics were no longer effective, modern medicine as we know it today would no longer be possible at all.".

    It has been revealed that imirzalioglu is not only an expert on antibiotic resistance but also on "One Health," a concept adopted in 2004 by experts in human medicine, veterinary medicine and nature conservation. It recognizes that the health of humans, animals and the environment is closely interconnected.

    After all, antibiotics and antimicrobial-resistant germs are not just a problem in hospitals. They can also be found in animal shelters, in animal products, in waste water, in fertilizers and in plants. "One Health tries to keep an eye on all of this," Imirzalioglu remarked.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    Industry observers note that for hospitals and doctors' offices this means that antibiotics must be used as selectively and purposefully as possible. To this end, research is focused primarily on developing better and faster diagnostic methods.

    Industry observers note that in Germany, antibiotics were frequently prescribed against respiratory or urinary tract infections, Imirzalioglu noted. But antibiotics are only effective against bacteria. If a virus causes the infection, they are ineffective.

    Nonetheless, every antibiotics dose has consequences: it damages our gut microbiome. This consists of billions of micro-organisms, primarily bacteria, which are essential for digestion, metabolism and the immune system. "If we damage the [bacteria], resistant pathogens can spread and take their place," Imirzalioglu remarked.

    Another problem was that such a spreading of resistant pathogens in the gut often went unnoticed and without causing symptoms, he added.

    So people became "carriers of resistant pathogens, which they, in turn, release back into their environment.".

    In a recent development, in this way, resistant pathogens make their way out of hospitals via toilets and sinks into wastewater and, from there, into the Baltic Sea, where they are ingested by wild birds. This pathway was traced in a study by Katharina Schaufler, a veterinarian and microbiologist at the Helmholtz Institute for One Health (HIOH).

    Antibiotics have not only been used in humans on a large scale over a long time, excessive use in veterinary medicine has also led to resistance to nearly all available antibiotics, Schaufler said.

    In 2006, an EU-wide ban on the use of antibiotics as growth promoters in animal feedcame into effect. Since then, antibiotics may only be applied as part of veterinary treatment.

    According to recent reports, the problem is that due to factory farming the use of antibiotics for medical purposes is a permanent necessity. The mere fact that animals live together in confined spaces causes infections to spread rapidly.

    Lack of space as well as boredom lead the animals to injure each other and this happens in an environment where, in Schaufler's words, "there's already a high level of bacterial pressure.".

    Recent findings suggest that through fertilizers, antibiotic-resistant pathogens enter the environment. "It has been proven that, for example, resistant bacteria can still be found on lettuce heads," the veterinarian said. Resistant bacteria were also found time and again on meat.

    To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

    In a recent development, national solutions are also falling short. In many countries, antibiotics are still a standard additive in animal feed, Schaufler remarked. And in such countries, antibiotics could be obtained in drugstores without prescriptions, Imirzalioglu added. Both say that all of this makes the global fight against antibiotic resistance more difficult.

    Political will is of the essence when it comes to combating antibiotic resistance. Imirzalioglu works at Guardian, a project funded by the German Federal Ministry of Research, Technology and Space.

    The aim of the project is to prevent outbreaks of diseases caused by resistant bacteria by monitoring and analyzing wastewater in the German state of Hesse.

    At EU level, Imirzalioglu is also an advisor at the Antimicrobial Resistance One Health Network. He sums up his experience with policymakers: "The experts and working groups have great ideas, and then these are often scaled back or stifled during the initial stages.".

    Perhaps the lack of political will so far is one of the reasons why the WHO's Nyemazi is issuing an appeal to every individual: Preventing antibiotic resistance means preventing infections, through hygiene, regular vaccinations and doctor's appointments as well as taking medications in accordance with prescriptions.

    This article was originally published in German.

    In a recent development, before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, mentioned it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. Negotiations between countries on which regulations to adopt and how to enforce them will likely drag on well beyond that. Additionally, room was left for some of those yet-to-be-adopted regulations to remain “optional.”.

    Humanitarian organizations and some countries see a need to urgently adopt legally binding rules as semi-autonomous weapons and drones have been responsible for a significant number of civilian deaths in conflicts around the globe, including in Ukraine, Gaza, and Sudan.

    According to NPR, Russia, Israel, and the US proved to be the primary obstructions:.

    On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting’s agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.

    The manufacturer says on its website that it was established within the structure of Russia's defence ministry in 2011 and since 2015 has been operating within the military construction complex.

    Finland's coast guard said it had been alerted to the attack at around 08:50 local time (06:50 GMT) on Saturday and that the cargo vessel had been located approximately 50km west of the island of Suursaari in the Gulf of Finland.

    This prompted "temporary aviation and maritime restrictions" around the area, Finnish border officials remarked.

    Shortly after the incident, Finland's defence ministry noted a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating the country's airspace, potentially linked to "rescue or tracking operations".

    A Russian rescue vessel approached the ship and was told by the crew that they did not need to be evacuated, Kaliningrad's governor wrote on Telegram, adding: "The crew is right now carrying out the necessary work and intends to continue on its way.".

    The Finnish Border Guard later remarked the crew had been evacuated to another Russian vessel that was now already en route to Russia. The Russian rescue vessel had remained at the location of the stricken ship.

    It added that no environmental damage had been detected and that there was no danger to maritime traffic or people.

    Kaliningrad is a Russian exclave that sits between Poland and Lithuania.

    Defence Minister Antti HÃ¤kkÃ¤nen said that the Finnish Border Guard were responsible for the investigation into the attack and were co-operating with other relevant authorities.

    Nato has also been informed, the defence ministry said.

    The Baltic Sea has become a flashpoint in the Russia-Ukraine war, triggered when Russia introduced a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Ukraine has recently ramped up its long-range attacks against Russia beyond the front lines.

    Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone strike hit a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland.

Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.

    Nearly 72,000 people have been evacuated from areas of Odisha in eastern India as Tropical Cyclone Akvan approaches land. Akvan is expected to make landfall on Friday between Narsapur and Puri, prompting cyclone warnings from the India Meteorological Department for north Andhra Pradesh, Yanam and south Odisha coasts. Peak wind gusts are expected to reach 70mph, with rainfall totals through Friday and Saturday potentially exceeding 200mm for northern coastal Andhra Pradesh and Odisha.

    After a yellow level 2 severe thunderstorm warning by the South African Weather Service on Tuesday, torrential rainfall and large hail were reported across parts of Johannesburg. The storms triggered flash flooding and caused infrastructure damage in the township of Soweto. One person died, while another remains missing after the severe storms.

    • Kirsten described this as “the tale of two Nvidias this week,” with the manufacturer’s current executives assuring investors, “Hey, we’ve got this.” At the same time, “You’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back, circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back.” (The company’s falling stock price certainly suggests that Wall Street isn’t feeling reassured.).
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We got two very different pictures of Nvidia this week, depending on whether you were focused on the company’s latest earnings report or the tech executives loudly calling for former CEO Jensen Huang’s return.

    On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Kirsten Korosec, Tim De Chant, and I discussed the latest news from the AI chipmaker, which reported soaring revenue and insisted that it has no aims for Huang to return.

    Kirsten described this as “the tale of two Nvidias this week,” with the manufacturer’s current executives assuring investors, “Hey, we’ve got this.” At the same time, “You’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back, circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back.” (The company’s falling stock price certainly suggests that Wall Street isn’t feeling reassured.).

    Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.

    Kirsten Korosec: Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China. This was coming directly from the interim CEO Colette Kress, and that coincides with the Trump administration also talking about closing off what we have discussed in the past, which is this idea of remote access — really closing and tightening all these restrictions [so] the chips can’t make it into China.

    What was happening is that data centers were being set up right outside, in countries like Malaysia and elsewhere, and then companies within China were remote accessing these chips, and so that’s now also been shut down.

    A lot is happening on the China front that is so much bigger than Nvidia, but Nvidia came out publicly and stated, “Nope, we’re shutting this part down.” I’ll be very curious to see if this changes, maybe in the first half of 2027.

    Industry observers note that tim De Chant: I’d love to be a fly on the wall in some of these Trump administration conversations, because they were much more stringent in terms of export controls at the end of the first Trump administration, and that continued through the Biden administration, where they really restricted Nvidia’s ability to export chips to China. I think that something changed in the last couple of years that really opened Nvidia’s ability to sell in the country.

    Anthony Ha: One of the things that really surprised me as we were preparing for this episode was [learning that critics] of Nvidia’s stance towards China estimate that 20% of their business comes from China.

    According to recent reports, and again, that’s not something you’re going to see directly in their financials, because that’s not direct sales to Chinese companies. But they’re saying, “A lot of the chips that are getting sold to companies in Malaysia or other companies in East Asia or Southeast Asia are going to end up [used by companies in] China eventually.” And so that could be — if Nvidia is really serious about this, I think this is something that’s very much in flux — that could actually be a pretty significant blow to their bottom line.

    Sources indicate that kirsten: Although Nvidia’s bottom line is doing just fine. In every possible way, their guidance was incredible. They beat expectations. They have a long pipeline.

    It was really interesting because you have that happening, and then you have all this noise happening in social media, and also a number of other tech conferences were happening this past week — Dealbook Summit, there [were] a few others in which you had the highest profile people that you can think of in the tech world commenting on Jensen [Huang], and Jensen himself commenting.

    Recent findings suggest that so it’s like the tale of two Nvidias this week. You’ve got the earnings and the current executives really talking about, “Hey, we’ve got this.” In fact, that was the last line that Collette Kress remarked [on the earnings call]. And then at the exact same time, or in parallel, you’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back, circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back. So it’s really quite the drama that we are definitely not done with, by the way.

    In a recent development, anthony: Although I think that what the folks who’d like to see Jensen Huang come back would say is that this most recent quarter is the last quarter under him. This is the [last of the] good times that we’re seeing under him. And so we don’t know how well Nvidia will do without him.

    Sources indicate that it seems like Nvidia’s public stance right now [on Huang’s possible return] is, “No, that’s not happening.” But Nvidia’s public stance a week and a half before that was, “We stand behind Jensen. We have every confidence in his leadership.”.

    So depending on the various pressures on them, you can imagine that changing. I don’t know what it would take for that to happen. I don’t necessarily think it’s that likely, but I also don’t think that just because they’re saying it’s not happening now doesn’t mean it will never happen.

    Kirsten:  Sure, never say never.

    In a recent development, tim: Right, never say never. I do think that to some extent, their steadfastness and how swiftly they shot down the petitions asking for Jensen to return suggests there’s maybe a little bit more going on behind the scenes than we know on the outside. So that’s probably something to watch in the coming weeks.

    Kirsten: I think that the board is trying to be in control here, and they don’t want to be forced into a decision because someone like Elon Musk is saying that it needs to happen. And so, even if there is a day in which Jensen returns — which I think is pretty unlikely, especially because the investigation into how much and who knew what about chips being sold, allegedly, secretly to China. We don’t know the full picture of that yet.     💡 Key Takeaways

    • Amazon is taking its accusations that the Council is driving up prices offline and onto your packages.
    • Sources indicate that amazon is leaving no venue unexplored in its fight against the Newly introduced York City Council and the Delivery Protection Act.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Amazon is taking its accusations that the Council is driving up prices offline and onto your packages.

    Amazon is taking its accusations that the Council is driving up prices offline and onto your packages.

    Sources indicate that amazon is leaving no venue unexplored in its fight against the Newly introduced York City Council and the Delivery Protection Act. The company is now putting labels on shipments claiming that the Council could add up to $5 to any Amazon order. The Delivery Protection Act would effectively ban the sort of third-party arrangements Amazon right now uses to deliver many packages, including small companies and independent contractors. Last-mile delivery firms operating warehouses would need to be licensed by the city and directly employ their workers.

    Earlier this week, Amazon started showing notifications in its mobile app and on its website reading “Attention NYC Council could add up to $5 per order.” Now the firm is including an almost identical message on shipping labels.

    Amazon claims that the bill, if passed, “would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in Upcoming York City,” and has threatened to move its warehouses outside of the city. However, labor unions, Council Speaker Julie Menin, and Mayor Zohran Mamdani have countered that the company is attempting to “threaten New Yorkers and intimidate this City Council” and is acting out of “greed,” pointing to Amazon’s market cap of nearly $3 trillion.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Wes Streeting told Volodymyr Zelensky he was in Kyiv to show that Europe was united in its support for Ukraine.
    • Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.
    • Sources indicate that in comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Wes Streeting told Volodymyr Zelensky he was in Kyiv to show that Europe was united in its support for Ukraine.

    Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has justified Kyiv's repeated attacks on a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, calling it a "fair response" to 109 separate Russian attacks on bridges in Ukraine.

    Sources indicate that in comments to the BBC in Kyiv, Zelensky said the intense attacks on Ukraine by Russia that have followed the strikes on the Crimean Bridge were only a "signal that Vladimir Putin does not want to stop. He wants a reason to escalate".

    He rejected the claim by the Russian president that the bridge - which links Russia to the peninsula it illegally annexed from Ukraine - was "exclusively civilian" in use.

    "There are facts, not just the words of Putin. We can see," he said.

    The Ukrainian president pointed to images online of tanks and other Russian military hardware using the route from Russia into occupied Crimea as a supply line and for logistics.

    "If Putin used the internet, he could see that.".

    The Ukrainian president added that Russia had carried out attacks with missiles and drones on bridges in Ukraine.

    This week's combined missile-and-drone strikes by Ukrainian forces destroyed the central road section of the Crimean Bridge, collapsing part of it together with one of the two support arches into the sea and rendering the structure unusable for road traffic.

    Industry observers note that russian attacks on Ukraine continued on Friday evening and overnight: a seven-year-old boy was killed in missile and drone strikes on Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih in the central Dnipropetrovsk region. Local officials say he had been in a playground at the time.

    A 20-year-old female medic was also killed. A local official added that when rescuers rushed to the scene, the same site was targeted again with jet powered drones. Another 58 people were injured in the city.

    Ukraine's state emergency service DSNS remarked 11 people were also injured in the north-eastern Kharkiv region, and one person in Rivne, in the north-west.

    Russia debuted its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

    Footage reveals Ukrainian missile approach Crimean Bridge.

    Zelensky was speaking ahead of a meeting in Kyiv with UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who told the Ukrainian president he was here to show that Europe was united in its support.

    "The more Putin tries to divide us, the more resolute we become," Streeting said.

    He remarked that Russian missiles hitting Poland on Friday, during military exercises of the so-called Coalition of the Willing, was an "outrageous provocation".

    The timing, Streeting mentioned, seemed "more than a coincidence".

    Asked by the BBC about Nato's response, he said the best way was to "do more for Ukraine" to defend itself against Putin who he called a "cold-blooded killer".

    Recent findings suggest that streeting's description of Putin chimed with the comments made earlier by Zelensky, who described the Kremlin leader a "killer". This was done in response to US President Donald Trump referring this week to Putin as his "friend".

    Streeting's visit to Kyiv came after European leaders meeting in Berlin on Thursday alongside US envoys remarked they were ready for negotiations with Moscow on ending the war in Ukraine.

    "Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham mentioned, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".

    Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president - who had also dialled into the meeting from Air Force One - wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side".

    Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks - but earlier this week he invited European representatives to Moscow as it wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".

    That meeting in the German capital came hours after Putin had held historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, China, with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

    Zelensky stated he had been "sceptical" ahead of the latest round of talks, when US envoys claimed that Russia was prepared to make compromises to end the war.

    "I thought [Putin] would find reason to escalate.".

    Sources indicate that speaking to the BBC, Streeting added: "Putin has absolutely no business playing the victim. He is the aggressor in this war. He provoked an illegal invasion of Ukraine. And all of us, right throughout the world, need to judge Putin not on his words, but on his actions.".

    In a separate development on Saturday, Finland mentioned it "detected a drone strike on a Russian merchant vessel" in the eastern Gulf of Finland, "in an international maritime area".

    The Finnish defence ministry stated in a statement that the vessel was damaged, without giving any further details.

    It added that "temporary restrictions on aviation and maritime areas in the eastern Gulf of Finland" were now reinstated for safety reasons.

    Russia has not publicly commented on the issue.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Signal revealed Friday that it’s limiting customers’ ability to take screenshots within the secure messaging app — a response to what President Meredith Whittaker described as the “existential threat” of operating systems that integrate agentic AI.
    • Whittaker wrote that by giving AI agents the ability to “scan” the information on people’ screens, Windows, Android, and macOS/iOS “are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.”.
    • According to recent reports, “Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” she mentioned.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Signal revealed Friday that it’s limiting customers’ ability to take screenshots within the secure messaging app — a response to what President Meredith Whittaker described as the “existential threat” of operating systems that integrate agentic AI.

    Whittaker wrote that by giving AI agents the ability to “scan” the information on people’ screens, Windows, Android, and macOS/iOS “are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.”.

    According to recent reports, “Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” she mentioned. “All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.”.

    Signal already sought to limit these risks by blocking screenshots of its Windows app by default. Now it’s adding similar restrictions in Android and iOS.

    That mentioned, consumers can disable this setting if they wish, which Whittaker said would “break our privacy guarantees.” She also admitted this is an “incomplete” solution, as it doesn’t “address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data.”.
